name: Cow
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Cows have been kept since the Stone Age for farming, food, milk and draught work. Pakistan had about 39.7 million cows, 34.6 million buffaloes, 66.6 million goats and 29.1 million sheep (Economic Survey 2014); cows and buffaloes supply most of the meat. Each person needs about 27.4 g of animal protein a day but gets only about 17.4 g, so more milk and meat are needed. Information comes from the Livestock and Dairy Development Department, Punjab.
aspects.breeds:
Breed groups: dairy breeds Sahiwal, Red Sindhi and Cholistani; dual-purpose Tharparkar (Thari); hardy draught breeds Bhagnari, Dhanni, Rojhan, Lohani and Dajal.
Sahiwal: home is the Ganji Bar between the Sutlej and Ravi (Sahiwal, Okara, Multan, Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh), now spread across canal areas of Punjab. Reddish-brown, medium-heavy, loose skin; cows have a small head, drooping ears, heavy dewlap, short horns or none, a large udder and clear milk veins. Matures at about 26 months, first calf at about 38 months, about 650 litres per lactation.
Red Sindhi: from the Kohistan hills (parts of Karachi, Thatta, Dadu, Hyderabad, and Lasbela in Balochistan). Medium size, solid red body.
Cholistani: ancestor of Sahiwal; from the Cholistan desert (Bahawalpur, Bahawalnagar, Rahim Yar Khan). Medium size, white with brown or black spots. Cows give milk; male calves are raised for good meat.
Tharparkar (Thari): from Tharparkar's sand dunes; tolerates poor fodder and harsh weather; light grey with a white stripe on the spine; good milker. Adult bulls 400 to 500 kg, cows 300 to 380 kg.
Dhanni: Attock, Chakwal, Rawalpindi, Jhelum, Mianwali, Sargodha. Medium size, many colour patterns (white with black spots, black with white spots, and others). Low milk.
Lohani: Loralai (Balochistan) and Dera Ismail Khan. Small, red with white spots, very hardy, tolerates shortage of fodder and water; low milk, kept for meat and light work in hilly areas. Bulls 300 to 350 kg, cows 230 to 280 kg.
Rojhan: hilly Dera Ghazi Khan and parts of Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan. Medium, sturdy, red and white; bulls for light draught in hilly areas.
Dajal: Dajal area of Dera Ghazi Khan, a branch of Bhagnari; grey or white, heavy build; low milk, bulls for heavy work.
Crossbred cows: cross local cows with exotic breeds (Friesian, Jersey) to combine high milk with local disease resistance and heat tolerance. Crossbreds mature at about 15 months, calve first at about 26 months and give 2,100 to 2,300 litres per lactation. Research at Bahadurnagar, Okara found 50 percent exotic blood best; keep exotic blood at 50 percent, not more or less. In milk competitions crossbred cows set records, e.g. 72.8 kg a day against 36 to 42 kg for Sahiwal.
Beef crosses (Bahadurnagar research since 1998): local cows crossed with Angus, Hereford, Charolais and Simmental. Calves weigh about 30 to 34 kg at birth, 194 to 225 kg at weaning, gain about 0.8 to 0.9 kg a day, and reach 260 to 305 kg at one year.
aspects.care:
Crossbred cows feel heat more than local cows: in hot weather graze them in the morning and evening, keep them under shady trees in the hot part of the day, and give plenty of fresh cool water. Shade trees work better than bathing or fans in a shed. Keep salt licks in the mangers. High-yielding cows can get mastitis at any time, so keep the shed very clean.
Calves: crossbred cows leave their calves easily, so calves can be raised separately and fed with a bottle and nipple. Keep young calves apart in individual pens: calves lick each other and swallow hair, which forms balls in the stomach and can kill them; eating soil brings worms; separate pens also reduce pneumonia and infections. Give clean water, protect from worms and weather, keep under shade in summer, and feed well up to 15 months.
A 50-cow farm needs about 6 workers, medicines and vaccines, an electric chaff cutter, milk cans and pails, a pickup, and about 30 acres for green and dry fodder.
aspects.shed:
Sheds for crossbred cows must be airy, with the length running east–west so cows don't suffer from summer heat. A simple roof on 12 brick pillars with T-iron or wooden beams makes a durable shed. Boundary wall strong but no higher than 5 feet so air can pass. Shed height 18 to 20 feet in the middle, 12 to 15 feet at the sides. Pucca floor and mangers, with the floor sloping toward the cows' hind feet and a drain at the end. Manger 2 feet wide and 2.5 feet high, with the back wall a little higher so fodder isn't wasted. Each cow needs 40 square feet of covered space and twice that as open yard, plus a water trough. Plant shade trees around the shed.
Calf pens: iron pens 5 feet long, 3 feet wide and 3 feet high, with 9-inch legs so the floor is raised; easy to clean and to move.
A 50-cow farm (50 cows, 1 bull, 20 young stock over a year, 35 suckling calves) needs about 3,340 square feet covered and 6,680 square feet open: about 10,020 square feet in total.
aspects.feed:
A cow needs on average 40 to 50 kg of green fodder a day; if short, make it up with wheat straw (toori), rice straw (parali) or concentrate (wanda). A cow giving 3 to 4 litres needs no concentrate if green fodder is enough; above that give 1 kg of balanced concentrate for every 3 litres of milk. In the last two months of pregnancy give 1.5 kg of balanced concentrate a day: the cow stays healthy, the calf is born healthy and she gives more milk.
Calves: for the first six weeks milk equal to 10 percent of body weight a day, then reduce gradually and stop at three months. Crossbred calves start eating fodder at about one month, so keep good green fodder in the manger; give heifers concentrate at 1 percent of body weight a day for good growth and early maturity.
Concentrate formula for milking cows (1): cottonseed cake 10, maize gluten feed 30% 18, wheat bran 34, cottonseed meal 8, toria meal 10, molasses 18, salt 1, bone meal or DCP 1 (percent). Formula (2): cottonseed cake 15, maize gluten feed 30% 15, wheat bran 20, cottonseed meal 5, rice polish 18, molasses 15, salt 1, DCP 1, mustard or toria cake 10.
Dry cows: toria cake 10, urea-treated wheat straw 60, bran 12, molasses 16, salt 1, bone meal/DCP 1.
Fattening calves (1): maize gluten feed 30% 24, wheat straw 32, wheat bran 16, urea 1, molasses 25, salt 1, bone meal/DCP 1. (2): mustard cake 10, wheat straw 36, wheat bran 20, urea 2, molasses 30, salt 1, bone meal 1.
Milk replacer for calves: cottonseed cake 35, molasses 25, barley or wheat porridge 20, mineral mix 0.5, maize gluten feed 20% 14, salt 0.5, wheat bran 14.
50-cow farm: green fodder 40 to 50 kg and wheat straw 3 to 5 kg per cow a day; concentrate 3 kg per milking cow for 280 days, 1.5 kg per pregnant cow for 60 days, 1 kg per heifer all year.
aspects.health:
Always get a diagnosis from a Livestock Department lab or a qualified vet before using any medicine, and vaccinate as the Livestock Department advises.
Foot and mouth disease (FMD, munh khur): high fever, blisters in the mouth and between the hooves, difficulty eating and walking, limping, less milk; very severe in crossbred and exotic cows. Vaccinate twice a year (February–March, and again August–October); immunity lasts six months. Wash sores with potassium permanganate and use antibiotics as advised.
Haemorrhagic septicaemia (HS, gal ghotu): high fever, stops eating and chewing cud, swollen throat, difficulty breathing; can kill by choking within hours. Vaccinate in May–June and again November–December (HS vaccine); immunity lasts six months. Antibiotics such as oxytetracycline are used.
Black quarter (chorray maar): hot, painful swelling on the thigh or shoulder that crackles when pressed; the animal limps. Vaccinate in February–March (March–April); immunity lasts a year.
Anthrax (goli, sut): high fever, restlessness, red swollen eyes, blood in dung and urine; the animal is often found dead without signs, and blood from body openings doesn't clot. The vaccine protects for a year.
Lumpy skin disease: lumps on the skin, fever, watery eyes. Vaccinate, give painkiller and antibiotic as advised, and control flies and mosquitoes.
Mastitis (thanaila): swollen, painful udder, milk with blood or pus. Use antibiotic cream and injections as advised and keep the udder clean.
Ticks: vaccinate against FMD; use Novagon or Asuntol against ticks on a vet's advice.
aspects.deworming: Worms (round, tape and flat worms) cause weakness, loose dung, a dull rough coat, weight loss, swelling under the jaw, less milk and meat, and diarrhoea with blood, worms or mucus; they cause malnutrition, anaemia and blocked intestines and lower immunity. Rainy season and open grazing increase them. Get dung samples tested at a lab and use dewormers such as albendazole or ivermectin as the vet directs.
aspects.milking: Some crossbred cows give more than 20 to 25 litres a day; milking them three times a day, eight hours apart, eases udder pressure and raises milk yield. Their feed needs are higher too. If milk smells, mix 20 g of baking soda into the fodder daily for one week. Dhanni, Lohani and Dajal cows give little milk.
aspects.breeding: To keep 50 percent exotic blood: breed local cows with exotic bulls, and breed 50 percent crossbred cows with 50 percent crossbred bulls, using artificial insemination. Use ordinary local cows for crossbreeding. Crossbreds mature at about 15 months and calve first at about 26 months (Sahiwal: about 26 and 38 months). For more beef, crossing local cows with beef breeds (Angus, Hereford, Charolais, Simmental) gives faster-growing calves.
aspects.other: Each person in Pakistan gets about 10 g less animal protein a day than needed; more milk and meat from cows and buffaloes can close the gap.
